name: Study: Cultural perceptions around gender roles remain an obstacle in early childhood education

content.text: This event brought together Early Childhood Care Education and Development (EC) specialists and stakeholders from across Tanzania, mainland and Zanzibar, and scholars from the East African region to engage with the findings from the TWW project and chart possible ways forward to promote the development of EC services in Tanzania and the East African region at large.  Nearly 45 specialist EC practitioners across a range of constituencies - NGOs, Community-based organisations, higher and further education institutions and education training centres - attended the event. Two colleagues from IED-Pakistan were also able to participate - Dr Almina Pardhan and Cassandra Fernandes - enabling closer ties between the two IEDs to be nurtured in this important area of education.

As this is the first study of its kind to attempt to map EC education capacity across Tanzania, key objectives of this event were to provide an avenue for the dissemination of the TWW project findings, to seek feedback on these findings, to gain additional insights from the different sectors at the dialogue, as well as to stimulate debate among EC stakeholders.
The findings covered sensitive issues related to gender and leadership, standards and assessment, the lack of professionalization of EC teachers and carers, and issues of language.

Several participants discussed cultural perceptions around gender roles. For example, the opportunities available to men and women were different because of cultural perceptions about what men and women do. Men were seen to be in leadership positions because "men will always think they are strong and powerful" (HEI, Kilimajaro), while women take care of the home. Some participants suggested that others believe that the nature and attitude of women is more conducive to working with small children than in dealing with managerial tasks.

"It is more cultural than anything else ... it has something to do with our culture we believe women take care of children better than men it is an issue of gender ... we believe this vocation of nursery school can be taken care of better by women than men" (HEI, Mwanza)

On mainland Tanzania, universities, government and private TTC's all used government curricula. However, different books and teaching materials are used. One participant noted other existing gaps in the provision of ECE programs in the country to be a lack of uniformity around the standards used to assess their programmes.

We have found examples of 'best practice' that are focused on marginalized, vulnerable groups and children to special needs. However, focusing on a specific group leaves out large numbers of children who do not fall into these more urgent 'priority' categories. Thus, by default, significant numbers of children lose out on scaffolded development opportunities available for others. This in turn raises issues not only of quality for all but also access for all.

A major output of the project has been the development of a Compendium of over 800 publications that includes for the first time a considerable number of publications from Sub-Saharan Africa and by African scholars. This work, led by our Canadian research team members, Professor Alan Pence and Emily Ashton at the University of Victoria, provides a unique and seminal resource for the region.

Benedict Missani, Acting Director of Ministry of Community Development, Gender and Children "The whole thing is a very nice experience. For the first time the University sector is working closely with government and providing us with recommendations in areas important to early childhood."

The TWW Dialogue participants were encouraged to stay in touch with the research team at IED and in particular to contribute resources to be included on the webpages for TWW that have just been set up and to support the research team in keeping the Compendium current.

content.title: Study: Cultural perceptions around gender roles remain an obstacle in early childhood education
content.author: Hiba Khan
content.description: On 9th February 2015 the Tuwaendeleze Watoto Wetu (TWW, www.tww.or.tz) research team at IED-EA held its final dialogue brief. AKU-IED worked in very close partnership with the Tanzania Early Childhood Development Network, and with government Ministries, particularly with the Ministry of Community Development, Gender and Children during the project. Professor Alan Pence from the University of Victoria, Canada joined the team as Co-PI with IED's Professor Pauline Rea-Dickins.
